A token-ID masking intervention reduces phantom edits, indicating models possess the underlying reasoning capacity but are misled by tokenizer artifacts.
Most phantom edits (72.2%) preserve subtoken count (1→1 transitions) and are primarily due to whitespace-variant token pairs.
papers.limitation: The token-ID masking intervention is a post-hoc, superficial remedy that does not address the fundamental many-to-one mapping property of tokenization, and complete tokenizer redesign and model re-training remain computationally expensive.
future_direction: Test whether tokenization non-uniqueness affects reasoning behaviors beyond the replacement probe, such as chain-of-thought stability or multi-step arithmetic accuracy.
Develop tokenizer-aware training objectives that enforce representational consistency across equivalent encodings.
Redesign tokenizers to shrink equivalence classes, for example by eliminating duplicate forms of the same word.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reason over discrete token ID sequences, yet modern subword tokenizers routinely produce non-unique encodings: multiple token ID sequences can detokenize to identical surface strings. This representational mismatch creates an unmeasured fragility wherein reasoning processes can fail. LLMs may treat two internal representations as distinct "words" even when they are semantically identical at the text level. In this work, we show that tokenization can betray LLM reasoning through one-to-many token ID mappings. We introduce a tokenization-consistency probe that requires models to replace designated target words in context while leaving all other content unchanged. The task is intentionally simple at the surface level, enabling us to attribute failures to tokenizer-detokenizer artifacts rather than to knowledge gaps or parameter limitations. Through analysis of over 11000 replacement trials across state-of-the-art open-source LLMs, we find a non-trivial rate of outputs exhibit phantom edits: cases where models operate under the illusion of correct reasoning, a phenomenon arising from tokenizer-induced representational defects. We further analyze these cases and provide a taxonomy of eight systematic tokenizer artifacts, including whitespace-boundary shifts and intra-word resegmentation. These findings indicate that part of apparent reasoning deficiency originates in the tokenizer layer, motivating tokenizer-level remedies before incurring the cost of training ever-larger models on ever-larger corpora.

papers.title: Why Can't Transformers Learn Multiplication? Reverse-Engineering Reveals Long-Range Dependency Pitfalls
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication?
papers.core_contribution: By reverse-engineering a successful implicit chain-of-thought model, the paper uncovers that transformers fail at multiplication due to a lack of long-range dependencies, and demonstrates that an auxiliary loss providing the correct inductive bias can enable learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication due to a pitfall in learning long-range dependencies with gradient descent and an auto-regressive loss, but this can be addressed with the correct inductive bias, as demonstrated by the auxiliary loss method.
papers.key_findings:
The ICoT model learns the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication, while standard fine-tuning does not.
The ICoT model encodes long-range dependencies via attention patterns that form a directed acyclic graph (attention tree) to cache and retrieve pairwise partial products.
The ICoT model implements partial products in attention heads as Minkowski sums and represents digits using a Fourier basis, forming an efficient pentagonal prism structure.
Standard fine-tuning converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies, causing loss to plateau on middle digits.
An auxiliary loss that supervises the prediction of a 'running partial sum' via a linear regression probe provides an inductive bias that enables the model to learn multiplication successfully.
papers.limitation: The suggested inductive bias is task-specific and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Developing generalizing inductive biases for tasks with long-range dependencies.
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly capable, yet still fail at a seemingly simple task of multi-digit multiplication. In this work, we study why, by reverse-engineering a model that successfully learns multiplication via \emph{implicit chain-of-thought}, and report three findings: (1) Evidence of long-range structure: Logit attributions and linear probes indicate that the model encodes the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication. (2) Mechanism: the model encodes long-range dependencies using attention to construct a directed acyclic graph to ``cache'' and ``retrieve'' pairwise partial products. (3) Geometry: the model implements partial products in attention heads by forming Minkowski sums between pairs of digits, and digits are represented using a Fourier basis, both of which are intuitive and efficient representations that the standard fine-tuning model lacks. With these insights, we revisit the learning dynamics of standard fine-tuning and find that the model converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies. We further validate this understanding by introducing an auxiliary loss that predicts the ``running sum'' via a linear regression probe, which provides an inductive bias that enables the model to successfully learn multi-digit multiplication. In summary, by reverse-engineering the mechanisms of an implicit chain-of-thought model we uncover a pitfall for learning long-range dependencies in Transformers and provide an example of how the correct inductive bias can address this issue.

papers.title: From Next-Token to Mathematics: The Learning Dynamics of Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does mathematical reasoning ability develop during pre-training and post-training in LLMs, and how aligned are the learning trajectories with human curricula?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MathCAMPS, a fine-grained dataset for mathematical reasoning, and uses it to analyze learning dynamics, showing that mathematical skills are learned in an order correlated with human curriculum and that instruction tuning has varied effects on different skills.
papers.conclusion: MathCAMPS enables fine-grained analysis of mathematical reasoning, revealing insights into learning dynamics and the effects of instruction tuning, paving the way for an empirical understanding of LLM training dynamics in relation to reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Mathematical skills are learned during pre-training in an order that measurably correlates with the human-designed curriculum, even though training data are randomly ordered.
Skills evolve smoothly during training rather than emerging discretely at specific points.
Instruction tuning has varied effects: it improves some mathematical skills but degrades others, and the impact depends on the specific tuning methodology.
Models struggle more with fraction operations than with decimal operations, likely due to tokenization differences and the multi-step reasoning required for fractions.
Models are not robust to follow-up questions, showing significant accuracy drops when probed with incremental or counterfactual questions.
papers.limitation: The evaluation only covers computational problems and does not capture conceptual mathematical skills that human students also learn.
future_direction: Using MathCAMPS to inform model pre-training and evaluation for educational applications.
Using follow-up problems in MathCAMPS as a rich source for further analysis of model robustness and dialogue understanding.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) solely trained on next-token prediction learn to solve a wide range of problems involving mathematical reasoning. But how does this ability evolve during training? We show the first analysis of how mathematical reasoning abilities of several open-weight LLMs develop during pre-training and post-training. To this end, we construct MathCAMPS, a synthetic dataset of novel mathematical reasoning problems grounded in 44 fine-grained skills taken from the Common Core curriculum from K to 8th grades. In one experiment, we show that mathematical skills are learned during pre-training in an order that measurably correlates with the human-designed curriculum, even though training data are randomly ordered. We also show a detailed analysis of which mathematical abilities benefit from instruction tuning, a widely used post-training method and, in contrast, which skills suffer. Our work paves the way for an empirical understanding of LLM training dynamics in relation to reasoning.

papers.title: Probing for Arithmetic Errors in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal activations in language models be used to detect arithmetic errors?
papers.core_contribution: Simple probes can detect arithmetic errors from internal activations and enable lightweight self-correction via re-prompting.
papers.conclusion: Simple probes can extract predicted outputs and correct answers from internal activations, anticipate errors, generalize to chain-of-thought, and serve as weak oracles for self-correction.
papers.key_findings:
Probes can decode both the model's predicted output and the correct answer from hidden states with high accuracy.
Error detectors trained on these probes achieve over 90% accuracy in predicting model correctness.
Probes trained on simple arithmetic generalize to chain-of-thought reasoning on GSM8K problems.
Using error detectors to guide re-prompting corrects up to 11% of erroneous reasoning steps without degrading correct outputs.
Internal representations of numerical quantities are robust across contexts, enabling cross-setting generalization.
papers.limitation:
Focus on addition and subtraction, not other arithmetic operations like multiplication or division.
Experiments primarily on Gemma 2B IT, with limited evaluation on Phi-3.
Chain-of-thought analysis limited to addition-only GSM8K problems.
CoT evaluation uses structured equation formatting, not free-form natural language.
future_direction: Extend probing strategies to other arithmetic operations such as multiplication and division.
Broader evaluation across diverse architectures and model scales.
Explore other datasets with broader math coverage and varied reasoning formats.
Extend approach to operate over general, unstructured CoT traces.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether internal activations in language models can be used to detect arithmetic errors. Starting with a controlled setting of 3-digit addition, we show that simple probes can accurately decode both the model's predicted output and the correct answer from hidden states, regardless of whether the model's output is correct. Building on this, we train lightweight error detectors that predict model correctness with over 90% accuracy. We then extend our analysis to structured chain-of-thought traces on addition-only GSM8K problems and find that probes trained on simple arithmetic generalize well to this more complex setting, revealing consistent internal representations. Finally, we demonstrate that these probes can guide selective re-prompting of erroneous reasoning steps, improving task accuracy with minimal disruption to correct outputs. Our findings suggest that arithmetic errors can be anticipated from internal activations alone, and that simple probes offer a viable path toward lightweight model self-correction.

papers.title: The emergence of number and syntax units in LSTM language models
papers.research_question: How do LSTMs capture syntax-sensitive generalizations such as long-distance number agreement, and do they rely on heuristics or genuine syntactic processing mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that long-distance number agreement in LSTMs is managed by specialized 'number units' and a 'syntax unit', providing direct evidence that LSTMs learn genuine syntactic processing mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: LSTMs trained on unannotated corpus data learn to perform structure-dependent linguistic operations, suggesting that raw linguistic input and generic memory mechanisms may suffice to induce non-trivial grammatical rules.
papers.key_findings:
Two 'number units' (singular and plural) encode and store grammatical number information across long-range dependencies.
A 'syntax unit' encodes the main subject-verb dependency and controls the gates of the number units via strong afferent connections.
Number is also encoded in a distributed manner by short-range units, but these are not syntax-sensitive and are affected by intervening nouns.
The interaction between syntax and number units suggests that LSTMs learn structure-based syntactic representations, not just superficial heuristics.
The study provides a mechanistic understanding of how LSTMs perform long-distance number agreement at the single neuron level.
papers.limitation:
The study excludes agreement across relative clauses, which adds complexity.
The analysis is limited to a single LSTM model and English, and may not generalize to other architectures, languages, or domains.
future_direction: Explore how the encoding pattern varies across network architectures, hyperparameters, languages, and domains.
Investigate the timecourse of emergence of the found behaviour over training time.
Test predictions on human brain dynamics to see if similar distinctions between short-range and long-range units exist.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that LSTMs trained on a generic language modeling objective capture syntax-sensitive generalizations such as long-distance number agreement. We have however no mechanistic understanding of how they accomplish this remarkable feat. Some have conjectured it depends on heuristics that do not truly take hierarchical structure into account. We present here a detailed study of the inner mechanics of number tracking in LSTMs at the single neuron level. We discover that long-distance number information is largely managed by two `number units'. Importantly, the behaviour of these units is partially controlled by other units independently shown to track syntactic structure. We conclude that LSTMs are, to some extent, implementing genuinely syntactic processing mechanisms, paving the way to a more general understanding of grammatical encoding in LSTMs.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Expanding Computation Spaces of LLMs at Inference Time
papers.research_question: Whether language models can leverage artificially inserted sequences of filler tokens solely at inference time as expanded computation spaces, and how token types, numbers, insertion locations, training stage, and attention dynamics affect this.
papers.core_contribution: Language models can exploit filler tokens inserted at inference as expanded computation spaces to improve performance on QA and math tasks, with smaller models benefiting more, and attention analysis shows these spaces engage in meaningful computation.
papers.conclusion: Inserting filler tokens at inference provides expanded computation spaces that improve model performance, especially for smaller models, and these spaces are used meaningfully for answer inference as shown by attention analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models (e.g., 1.7B) benefit most from inserted filler tokens, with gains up to 12.372 percentage points, suggesting the spaces compensate for limited parameter capacity.
Optimal token types and counts vary across models; placing filler tokens directly before the final 'Answer:' token is most effective.
Models progressively learn to leverage these spaces during pretraining and instruction-tuning, as shown by checkpoint analysis.
Attention map analysis reveals filler tokens attend to questions and answer options, influencing answer selection, rather than being redundant.
Performance degrades sharply when too many tokens (e.g., >1024) are added, resembling the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades when too many filler tokens are added, as models are not trained on such inputs.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) rationale enables language models to use additional task-related text for problem-solving, benefiting not only from detailed reasoning steps but also from the expanded computational space of longer inputs. Prior work has trained filler or special tokens to serve as additional computation spaces. In this study, we investigate whether language models can leverage artificially inserted sequences of filler tokens solely at inference. We first identify effective token types, numbers, and insertion locations, then examine at what stage of training models begin to exploit the expanded computation space, and finally analyze dynamics within these spaces via attention maps. Experiments on models ranging from 1.7B to 32B across open-domain QA and math tasks show that appropriate token types and counts vary, but placing filler tokens directly before the final 'Answer:' token is most effective. Smaller models benefit most, up to 12.372 percentage points in SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, indicating that these spaces act as additional computational capacity rather than redundant input. Attention maps reveal that expanded spaces often continue the original attention mechanism and sometimes focus on questions or answer options, suggesting meaningful computation for problem-solving.

papers.title: CircuitSeer: Mining High-Quality Data by Probing Mathematical Reasoning Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we select high-quality reasoning data for fine-tuning LLMs by leveraging the model's internal mechanisms, specifically sparse, specialized attention circuits, instead of relying on external heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CircuitSeer, a data selection method that quantifies reasoning complexity by measuring the influence of training samples on sparse, specialized attention head circuits identified within a reference LLM, enabling efficient fine-tuning with small, high-quality subsets.
papers.conclusion: CircuitSeer provides an interpretable, model-internal signal for reasoning data quality, enabling efficient and effective data selection for fine-tuning LLMs, and demonstrates that internal reasoning circuits encode measurable structures of problem difficulty.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse, specialized subset of attention heads forms core reasoning circuits that are consistently activated during complex mathematical reasoning tasks.
Fine-tuning on just 10% of data selected by CircuitSeer can outperform training on the full dataset, achieving a 1.4-point gain in average Pass@1 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B.
Scoring based on input problem statements (rather than output reasoning traces) more effectively captures reasoning complexity.
Soft sampling based on CircuitSeer scores yields better performance and diversity than deterministic top-k selection.
The identified reasoning heads provide a clearer signal for data selection than using all heads or a random subset.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities, but scaling their performance often relies on massive reasoning datasets that are computationally expensive to train on. Existing data selection methods aim to curate smaller, high-quality subsets but often rely on costly external models or opaque heuristics. In this work, we shift the focus from external heuristics to the model's internal mechanisms. We find that complex reasoning tasks consistently activate a sparse, specialized subset of attention heads, forming core reasoning circuits. Building on this insight, we propose CircuitSeer, a novel data selection method that quantifies the reasoning complexity of data by measuring its influence on these crucial circuits. Extensive experiments on 4 models and 9 datasets demonstrate CircuitSeer's superiority. Notably, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-7B on just 10% of data selected by our method achieves a 1.4-point gain in average Pass@1 over training on the full dataset, highlighting its efficiency and effectiveness.

papers.title: Can LLMs Reason Abstractly Over Math Word Problems Without CoT? Disentangling Abstract Formulation From Arithmetic Computation
papers.research_question: Does final-answer accuracy in math word problems conflate abstract formulation and arithmetic computation? What is the internal mechanism of LLMs when solving such problems without chain-of-thought?
papers.core_contribution: Disentangled evaluation shows that without CoT, models' final-answer accuracy is bottlenecked by arithmetic computation, not abstract formulation, and mechanistic analysis reveals an abstract-then-compute mechanism in a single forward pass.
papers.conclusion: Disentangled evaluation reveals that without CoT, models perform better at abstraction than computation, challenging the view that poor performance always implies reasoning failure. Mechanistic interpretability uncovers an abstract-then-compute mechanism with transferable abstractions, arguing for disentangled evaluation to assess model abilities more precisely.
papers.key_findings:
Without CoT, models perform better at abstract formulation than arithmetic computation, with computation being the main bottleneck for final-answer accuracy.
CoT primarily improves computation, with limited gains in abstract formulation.
Models use an abstract-then-compute mechanism in a single forward pass, where abstractions are formed first and then used for computation.
Abstractions are transferable across problem variants and can be composed with subsequent computation.
The abstract-then-compute mechanism is consistent across different models and problem types.
papers.limitation:
Focus solely on English-language datasets.
Evaluation decomposes mathematical problem-solving into only two stages: abstract formulation and arithmetic computation.
Interpretability analysis is limited to single-step generation.
Detailed analysis of components (e.g., attention heads, MLP neurons) is left for future work.
Analysis is limited to models up to 12B parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Extending interpretability techniques to multi-step reasoning.
Extending analysis to larger models.
Investigating finer-grained breakdowns of mathematical problem-solving.
papers.abstract: Final-answer-based metrics are commonly used for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on math word problems, often taken as proxies for reasoning ability. However, such metrics conflate two distinct sub-skills: abstract formulation (capturing mathematical relationships using expressions) and arithmetic computation (executing the calculations). Through a disentangled evaluation on GSM8K and SVAMP, we find that the final-answer accuracy of Llama-3 and Qwen2.5 (1B-32B) without CoT is overwhelmingly bottlenecked by the arithmetic computation step and not by the abstract formulation step. Contrary to the common belief, we show that CoT primarily aids in computation, with limited impact on abstract formulation. Mechanistically, we show that these two skills are composed conjunctively even in a single forward pass without any reasoning steps via an abstract-then-compute mechanism: models first capture problem abstractions, then handle computation. Causal patching confirms these abstractions are present, transferable, composable, and precede computation. These behavioural and mechanistic findings highlight the need for disentangled evaluation to accurately assess LLM reasoning and to guide future improvements.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Emergent Symbol-like Number Variables in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What types of numeric representations emerge in neural systems, and how can we interpret neural network solutions through the lens of interpretable Symbolic Algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: We extend the Distributed Alignment Search framework with alignment functions to interpret neural network activity in terms of symbolic variables, and show that recurrent networks develop graded symbol-like number variables while transformers use anti-Markovian solutions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the utility of causal interpretability tools and alignment functions for understanding neural representations, showing that RNNs develop graded symbol-like number variables while transformers use anti-Markovian solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrent models (GRUs/LSTMs) develop graded symbol-like number variables within their neural activity.
Seemingly insignificant task variations can drastically affect alignment to Symbolic Algorithms, motivating extended DAS with alignment functions (LAFs).
Linear Alignment Functions (LAFs) can control NN behavior through neural activity aligned to interpretable Symbolic Algorithms.
Shallow Transformers use anti-Markovian solutions to numeric tasks, and theoretically, Transformers must use anti-Markovian solutions without sufficient attention layers.
Causal interventions on neural subspaces are useful for NN interpretability.
papers.abstract: What types of numeric representations emerge in neural systems, and what would a satisfying answer to this question look like? In this work, we interpret Neural Network (NN) solutions to sequence based number tasks using a variety of methods to understand how well we can interpret them through the lens of interpretable Symbolic Algorithms (SAs) -- precise programs describable by rules and typed, mutable variables. We use autoregressive GRUs, LSTMs, and Transformers trained on tasks where the correct tokens depend on numeric information only latent in the task structure. We show through multiple causal and theoretical methods that we can interpret raw NN activity through the lens of simplified SAs when we frame the activity in terms of neural subspaces rather than individual neurons. Using Distributed Alignment Search (DAS), we find that, depending on network architecture, dimensionality, and task specifications, alignments with SA's can be very high, or they can be only approximate, or fail altogether. We extend our analytic toolkit to address the failure cases by expanding the DAS framework to a broader class of alignment functions that more flexibly capture NN activity in terms of interpretable variables from SAs, and we provide theoretic and empirical explorations of Linear Alignment Functions (LAFs) in contrast to the preexisting Orthogonal Alignment Functions (OAFs). Through analyses of specific cases we confirm the usefulness of causal interventions on neural subspaces for NN interpretability, and we show that recurrent models can develop graded, symbol-like number variables in their neural activity. We further show that shallow Transformers learn very different solutions than recurrent networks, and we prove that such models must use anti-Markovian solutions -- solutions that do not rely on cumulative, Markovian hidden states -- in the absence of sufficient attention layers.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: Emergent Specialization: Rare Token Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal mechanisms specialized for processing rare tokens during pre-training, and what are the mechanisms for their emergence and behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies rare token neurons in language models and shows they emerge through a three-phase structure during training, with coordinated activation and heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting a statistical mechanical basis for emergent specialization.
papers.conclusion: Language models spontaneously develop functionally specialized subnetworks for rare token processing, characterized by a three-phase structure and heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting emergent specialization analogous to biological complementary learning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop dedicated 'rare token neurons' that disproportionately impact the prediction of infrequent tokens.
These specialized neurons emerge through distinct phase transitions during training, evolving from a homogeneous initial state to a functionally differentiated architecture.
The emergence of specialized neuron groups correlates with the development of heavy-tailed weight distributions.
Rare token neurons form a coordinated subnetwork that selectively co-activates while avoiding co-activation with other neurons.
Neuron influence exhibits a three-phase structure: an influential plateau, a power-law decay phase, and a rapid decay phase.
papers.limitation:
Focus on final MLP layer only, while rare token processing likely involves distributed mechanisms across multiple architectural components.
Reliance on ablation-based proxies to quantify neuron contributions, which lack the theoretical rigor of more principled attribution methods.
Constrained to next-token prediction in autoregressive language modeling, so generalizability to downstream applications is unclear.
future_direction: Examining attention heads, intermediate layers, and cross-layer interactions to provide a more comprehensive understanding of rare token processing mechanisms.
Developing precise theoretical frameworks for measuring neuron-level effects to strengthen mechanistic interpretations.
Investigating rare token processing mechanisms in downstream applications such as question-answering and mathematical reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models struggle with representing and generating rare tokens despite their importance in specialized domains. In this study, we identify neuron structures with exceptionally strong influence on language model's prediction of rare tokens, termed as rare token neurons, and investigate the mechanism for their emergence and behavior. These neurons exhibit a characteristic three-phase organization (plateau, power-law, and rapid decay) that emerges dynamically during training, evolving from a homogeneous initial state to a functionally differentiated architecture. In the activation space, rare token neurons form a coordinated subnetwork that selectively co-activates while avoiding co-activation with other neurons. This functional specialization potentially correlates with the development of heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting a statistical mechanical basis for emergent specialization.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: A Sentence is Worth a Thousand Pictures: Can Large Language Models Understand Hum4n L4ngu4ge and the W0rld behind W0rds?
papers.research_question: Are humans and LLMs equally accurate in decoding leetspeak, and can they equally explain the substitutions?
papers.core_contribution: Humans outperform LLMs in decoding leetspeak, demonstrating that LLMs lack top-down processing and grounded cognition, which are essential for human-like language understanding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do not possess human-like linguistic competence; superficial similarity in output does not imply system equivalence, and models lack grounded cognition and top-down processing.
papers.key_findings:
Humans achieve near-ceiling accuracy in decoding leetspeak, while LLMs perform worse.
ChatGPT-4o is the best-performing model but still below humans, especially with more substitutions.
LLMs show an accuracy-reasoning mismatch, often decoding correctly but failing to explain substitutions.
Model errors are qualitatively different from human errors, indicating a lack of common sense and real-world grounding.
Performance differences suggest LLMs rely on form-based associations rather than meaning.
future_direction: Future language models may need to take an entirely different approach, beginning with deeper semantics and cognitive models of the world.
A closer examination of how LLM outputs align with subtle syntactic, acceptability judgments in humans.
Combining deep learning with models of symbolic cognition.
papers.abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence applications show great potential for language-related tasks that rely on next-word prediction. The current generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been linked to claims about human-like linguistic performance and their applications are hailed both as a step towards artificial general intelligence and as a major advance in understanding the cognitive, and even neural basis of human language. To assess these claims, first we analyze the contribution of LLMs as theoretically informative representations of a target cognitive system vs. atheoretical mechanistic tools. Second, we evaluate the models' ability to see the bigger picture, through top-down feedback from higher levels of processing, which requires grounding in previous expectations and past world experience. We hypothesize that since models lack grounded cognition, they cannot take advantage of these features and instead solely rely on fixed associations between represented words and word vectors. To assess this, we designed and ran a novel 'leet task' (l33t t4sk), which requires decoding sentences in which letters are systematically replaced by numbers. The results suggest that humans excel in this task whereas models struggle, confirming our hypothesis. We interpret the results by identifying the key abilities that are still missing from the current state of development of these models, which require solutions that go beyond increased system scaling.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Visualisation and 'Diagnostic Classifiers' Reveal How Recurrent and Recursive Neural Networks Process Hierarchical Structure
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics, specifically whether they can compute the meaning of nested arithmetic expressions and how they do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces diagnostic classifiers as a method to analyze internal representations of recurrent neural networks and shows that GRUs follow a cumulative strategy for processing hierarchical arithmetic expressions.
papers.conclusion: Diagnostic classifiers can open the black box of neural networks and reveal the strategies they use, with GRUs approximating a cumulative strategy for processing hierarchical structure.
papers.key_findings:
TreeRNNs learn a recursive solution to compute arithmetic expressions and generalize to longer expressions.
GRUs can learn to compute arithmetic expressions and generalize, but performance deteriorates with length.
Diagnostic classifiers reveal that GRUs follow a strategy similar to a cumulative strategy, not a recursive strategy.
The method of diagnostic classifiers is proposed as a scalable way to analyze high-dimensional RNNs.
Visualization techniques like project-sum-squash provide insight into the TreeRNN's composition function.
papers.limitation:
Diagnostic classifiers for gates may require more complex architectures to handle non-linearities.
The analysis is on an idealized task and has not been applied to deeper networks and real-world tasks.
The network's strategy deviates from the perfect cumulative strategy, especially for right-branching expressions.
future_direction: Using diagnostic classifiers for gates with non-linear architectures.
Applying diagnostic classification to higher-dimensional networks and real-world tasks like language modeling and machine translation.
Further research into the reasons for the mismatch between the network's strategy and the cumulative strategy for right-branching expressions.
papers.abstract: We investigate how neural networks can learn and process languages with hierarchical, compositional semantics. To this end, we define the artificial task of processing nested arithmetic expressions, and study whether different types of neural networks can learn to compute their meaning. We find that recursive neural networks can implement a generalising solution to this problem, and we visualise this solution by breaking it up in three steps: project, sum and squash. As a next step, we investigate recurrent neural networks, and show that a gated recurrent unit, that processes its input incrementally, also performs very well on this task: the network learns to predict the outcome of the arithmetic expressions with high accuracy, although performance deteriorates somewhat with increasing length. To develop an understanding of what the recurrent network encodes, visualisation techniques alone do not suffice. Therefore, we develop an approach where we formulate and test multiple hypotheses on the information encoded and processed by the network. For each hypothesis, we derive predictions about features of the hidden state representations at each time step, and train 'diagnostic classifiers' to test those predictions. Our results indicate that the networks follow a strategy similar to our hypothesised 'cumulative strategy', which explains the high accuracy of the network on novel expressions, the generalisation to longer expressions than seen in training, and the mild deterioration with increasing length. This in turn shows that diagnostic classifiers can be a useful technique for opening up the black box of neural networks. We argue that diagnostic classification, unlike most visualisation techniques, does scale up from small networks in a toy domain, to larger and deeper recurrent networks dealing with real-life data, and may therefore contribute to a better understanding of the internal dynamics of current state-of-the-art models in natural language processing.

papers.title: Small Vectors, Big Effects: A Mechanistic Study of RL-Induced Reasoning via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How does reasoning training reshape LLMs' internal computations, and what are the mechanisms of trainable steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Lightweight steering vectors trained with an RL objective explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving interpretability, and their mechanisms (e.g., token substitution at the last layer, MLP-mediated effects at the penultimate layer) are elucidated.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a compact and informative probe of reasoning-trained models, offering concrete insight into how RL-induced changes manifest in token preferences and internal circuitry.
papers.key_findings:
The last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, boosting tokens such as 'To' and 'Step'.
The penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and operates through the MLP and unembedding, up-weighting process words and structure symbols.
Steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family, suggesting underlying directions are preserved under fine-tuning.
Early-layer steering does not express later-layer steering directions; induced shifts diffuse and become nearly orthogonal to later-layer vectors.
Single-layer steering vectors isolate layer-specific effects and provide an upper bound on linear intervention performance at that layer.
papers.limitation: The effects are consistently stronger and cleaner in Qwen than in Llama, suggesting model-specific implementations of similar high-level behaviors.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across architectures and training recipes to explain differences in steering vector effects.
Pin down the precise mechanisms of mid-layer steering vectors, which are harder to localize to a single submodule.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which reasoning training reshapes LLMs' internal computations remain unclear. We study lightweight steering vectors inserted into the base model's residual stream and trained with a reinforcement-learning objective. These vectors explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving the interpretability of small, additive interventions. We find that (i) the last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, consistently boosting tokens such as "To" and "Step"; (ii) the penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and instead operates through the MLP and unembedding, preferentially up-weighting process words and structure symbols; and (iii) the steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family. Taken together, these results deepen understanding of how trained steering vectors shape computation and should inform future work in activation engineering and the study of reasoning models.

papers.title: Structure Development in List-Sorting Transformers
papers.research_question: How do neural networks develop organized internal structures as they learn? The paper answers this for a single-layer attention-only transformer model trained on sorting lists of numbers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows how a one-layer attention-only transformer develops organized internal structures (vocabulary-splitting and copy-suppression) while learning to sort lists, and identifies training data characteristics (distribution of gaps between sorted list elements) as a key driver of these specializations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how developmental interpretability can reveal the emergence of structured solutions in transformers, with training data characteristics playing a crucial role in determining the type of specialization that develops.
papers.key_findings:
The model undergoes distinct developmental stages: initial learning, head-overlapping, vocabulary-splitting, and sometimes copy-suppression.
Vocabulary-splitting represents a simpler solution (as measured by the Local Learning Coefficient) and occurs even without weight decay, suggesting neural networks have an inherent bias toward simpler solutions.
Copy-suppression arises in some settings and functions to calibrate the copying head, increasing model confidence in this case.
The distribution of gaps (δ) between adjacent list elements in the training data drives the type of head specialization: smaller mean δ and lower variance favor copy-suppression, while larger variance favors vocabulary-splitting.
The model's internal organization is shaped by features of the training data, providing a concrete example of how data influences learned structures.
papers.limitation: The study uses a toy model, which limits the direct applicability to larger models.
papers.abstract: We study how a one-layer attention-only transformer develops relevant structures while learning to sort lists of numbers. At the end of training, the model organizes its attention heads in two main modes that we refer to as vocabulary-splitting and copy-suppression. Both represent simpler modes than having multiple heads handle overlapping ranges of numbers. Interestingly, vocabulary-splitting is present regardless of whether we use weight decay, a common regularization technique thought to drive simplification, supporting the thesis that neural networks naturally prefer simpler solutions. We relate copy-suppression to a mechanism in GPT-2 and investigate its functional role in our model. Guided by insights from a developmental analysis of the model, we identify features in the training data that drive the model's final acquired solution. This provides a concrete example of how the training data shape the internal organization of transformers, paving the way for future studies that could help us better understand how LLMs develop their internal structures.

papers.title: Bottlenecked Transformers: Periodic KV Cache Consolidation for Generalised Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can periodic in-place rewrites of the KV cache (memory consolidation/reconsolidation) improve reasoning and generalization in Transformer LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Bottlenecked Transformer, which augments a backbone LLM with a Cache Processor that performs periodic, in-place KV cache rewrites (consolidation/reconsolidation) to improve reasoning performance, supported by information bottleneck theory.
papers.conclusion: Periodic KV cache rewrites via a Cache Processor improve reasoning performance in Transformer LLMs, and the mechanism is robust to hyperparameter choices.
papers.key_findings:
Bottlenecked Transformer improves over vanilla Transformers and pause-token baselines on math reasoning benchmarks, with gains up to +6.6pp.
Reconsolidation budget (k) and recent-step window (R) ablations show robust performance across moderate values.
Rewrite magnitudes show value vectors are updated more than keys, with edits concentrated in early layers.
Training budget comparison shows Bottlenecked Transformer often outperforms extra SFT epochs on most tasks.
The method is computationally expensive during training and currently incompatible with efficient attention like Flash Attention.
papers.limitation:
Computationally expensive during training (20x longer than SFT) and incompatible with efficient attention methods like Flash Attention.
May underperform on tasks requiring precise symbolic details or language-specific cues (e.g., MATH and Gaokao-MathQA).
future_direction: Extend to other domains beyond mathematical reasoning.
Improve training efficiency and integrate with efficient attention methods.
Explore different selection mechanisms for reconsolidation.
papers.abstract: Transformer LLMs have been shown to exhibit strong reasoning ability that scales with inference-time compute, most prominently through token-space "thinking" chains of thought. A growing line of work pushes extra computation into the model's latent space, which we term Auxiliary Latent-Space Computation (ALSC). Existing ALSC methods largely fall into three buckets: (i) token-mediated latent rollouts, (ii) residual/activation steering, and (iii) memory (KV) compression. An underexplored alternative is memory consolidation/reconsolidation, two processes in the brain that are responsible for stabilising newly formed memory traces, and, upon recall, transiently rendering established traces plastic such they can integrate new contextual information before restabilising. In Transformer LLMs, this can be seen as analogous to performing in-place rewrites of new KV segments, and rewrites of recalled past segments. In this work, we give a theoretical justification as to why memory (re)consolidation via KV cache rewrites is beneficial for improved reasoning. We do this through the lens of Information Bottleneck (IB) theory, which posits that model generalisation emerges from an optimal balance between input information compression and retention of predictive information in latent representations. We then introduce the Bottlenecked Transformer, which augments a backbone LLM with a Cache Processor, an auxiliary Transformer that performs periodic, non-causal, in-place KV rewrites at newline-delimited reasoning step boundaries. The Processor consolidates recently written KV entries and reconsolidates a small, top-k attention-selected set of prior entries. We evaluate our Bottlenecked Transformer architecture on math reasoning benchmarks. Our model sees consistent performance gains over vanilla Transformers and pause-token augmented baselines, with gains of up to +6.6pp for selected tasks/backbones.

papers.title: Interpreting Context Look-ups in Transformers: Investigating Attention-MLP Interactions
papers.research_question: How do attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly, providing a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads process context and use next-token neurons to help predict a word associated with, but not previously seen in that context, providing insight into how attention heads can work with MLP neurons to predict new words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads can recognize contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron.
An automated method can explain and characterize interactions between attention heads and token-predicting neurons.
The head explanation score can be used to evaluate the quality of explanations.
The phenomenon is observed across different model families and sizes (GPT-2 and Pythia variants).
Ablation experiments confirm that the identified attention heads are causally involved in predicting the token.
papers.limitation:
Focus on max-activating behavior of neurons, which might overlook subtler activation patterns.
Reliance on a maximum of 30 prompts per neuron.
GPT-4 struggles with longer prompts and may generate poor explanations for certain patterns (like induction-style prompts).
Scope limited to neurons whose associated tokens are whole words and prompts shorter than 100 tokens.
future_direction: Investigate whether this phenomenon happens to such neurons throughout their range of activations.
Look into whether multiple attention heads could work with a single next-token neuron.
Look into whether a single attention head could work with multiple next-token neurons.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for advancing their theoretical foundations and real-world applications. While the attention mechanism and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have been studied independently, their interactions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates how attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words. We propose a methodology to identify next-token neurons, find prompts that highly activate them, and determine the upstream attention heads responsible. We then generate and evaluate explanations for the activity of these attention heads in an automated manner. Our findings reveal that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly. This mechanism provides a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction. Our approach offers a foundation for further research into the intricate workings of LLMs and their impact on text generation and understanding.

papers.title: Sequential Enumeration in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can large language models robustly and systematically deploy counting procedures for sequential enumeration tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can perform sequential enumeration when explicitly instructed to count, but fail to do so spontaneously, indicating a lack of robust and systematic counting abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot yet robustly and systematically deploy counting procedures, highlighting a persistent gap between neural and symbolic approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Proprietary models achieve high accuracy in production tasks when explicitly asked to count.
Accuracy drops significantly in naming tasks and when counting is not explicitly instructed.
Models do not spontaneously engage in counting.
Internal dynamics show different computational strategies for explicit vs. mental counting.
Model size improves performance gradually but not emergently.
papers.limitation: LLMs do not spontaneously engage in counting when not explicitly instructed.
papers.abstract: Reliably counting and generating sequences of items remain a significant challenge for neural networks, including Large Language Models (LLMs). Indeed, although this capability is readily handled by rule-based symbolic systems based on serial computation, learning to systematically deploy counting procedures is difficult for neural models, which should acquire these skills through learning. Previous research has demonstrated that recurrent architectures can only approximately track and enumerate sequences of events, and it remains unclear whether modern deep learning systems, including LLMs, can deploy systematic counting procedures over sequences of discrete symbols. This paper aims to fill this gap by investigating the sequential enumeration abilities of five state-of-the-art LLMs, including proprietary, open-source, and reasoning models. We probe LLMs in sequential naming and production tasks involving lists of letters and words, adopting a variety of prompting instructions to explore the role of chain-of-thought in the spontaneous emerging of counting strategies. We also evaluate open-source models with the same architecture but increasing size to see whether the mastering of counting principles follows scaling laws, and we analyze the embedding dynamics during sequential enumeration to investigate the emergent encoding of numerosity. We find that some LLMs are indeed capable of deploying counting procedures when explicitly prompted to do so, but none of them spontaneously engage in counting when simply asked to enumerate the number of items in a sequence. Our results suggest that, despite their impressive emergent abilities, LLMs cannot yet robustly and systematically deploy counting procedures, highlighting a persistent gap between neural and symbolic approaches to compositional generalization.

papers.title: Positional Description Matters for Transformers Arithmetic
papers.research_question: How does positional encoding affect transformers' performance on arithmetic tasks, and how can we modify positional encoding or data representation to improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers' poor arithmetic performance stems from over-reliance on positional information, and proposes methods like padding, reversing products, and random embedding to improve performance, enabling small models to achieve high accuracy on large-digit multiplication and addition.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that with appropriate modifications to positional encoding or data format, small transformers can perform complex arithmetic tasks, highlighting the importance of positional information in arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Padding and reversing the product order enable a small transformer to perform 15-digit multiplication with high accuracy.
Using random spaces or recursive scratchpad formats improves length generalization in addition tasks.
Random embedding (a novel positional encoding) improves generalization for both digit reversion and addition tasks.
Integrating arithmetic data with natural language dialogue is challenging but can be improved by removing absolute positional embedding or using random embedding.
Including simple cases (like n×1 multiplication) in training helps models learn complex multiplication.
papers.limitation:
The experiments did not fine-tune hyperparameters, so higher accuracy for more digits might be possible with larger training sets, better digit distributions, or tuned learning rates.
The approaches for multiplication, length extrapolation, and natural language integration are tackled separately; a single model combining all properties is left for future work.
future_direction: Combining the proposed approaches into a single model that excels at all arithmetic challenges.
Exploring the methods on larger models and more complex arithmetic tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformers, central to the successes in modern Natural Language Processing, often falter on arithmetic tasks despite their vast capabilities --which paradoxically include remarkable coding abilities. We observe that a crucial challenge is their naive reliance on positional information to solve arithmetic problems with a small number of digits, leading to poor performance on larger numbers. Herein, we delve deeper into the role of positional encoding, and propose several ways to fix the issue, either by modifying the positional encoding directly, or by modifying the representation of the arithmetic task to leverage standard positional encoding differently. We investigate the value of these modifications for three tasks: (i) classical multiplication, (ii) length extrapolation in addition, and (iii) addition in natural language context. For (i) we train a small model on a small dataset (100M parameters and 300k samples) with remarkable aptitude in (direct, no scratchpad) 15 digits multiplication and essentially perfect up to 12 digits, while usual training in this context would give a model failing at 4 digits multiplication. In the experiments on addition, we use a mere 120k samples to demonstrate: for (ii) extrapolation from 10 digits to testing on 12 digits numbers while usual training would have no extrapolation, and for (iii) almost perfect accuracy up to 5 digits while usual training would be correct only up to 3 digits (which is essentially memorization with a training set of 120k samples).

papers.title: Three tiers of computation in transformers and in brain architectures
papers.research_question: What enabled transformer-based A.I. models to suddenly generate fluent natural language where previous AI models had failed, and why are current transformer-based models having difficulty obtaining arithmetic and logic skills?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark based on the grammar-automata hierarchy to evaluate computational capabilities, and provides a framework linking transitions in computational tiers to language and logic abilities in transformers and humans.
papers.conclusion: The grammar-automata hierarchy provides a principled framework for understanding the capabilities and limitations of transformers and humans, suggesting that architectural augmentations (like multiple memory stacks) are needed for logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs (under tens of billions of parameters) do not reliably process any of the formal grammar inputs.
Mid-sized LMs show some recognition of context-free grammar (CFG) but are unreliable on higher-level grammars.
Large LLMs and humans robustly recognize CFG and indexed grammar (IXG) strings, but not context-sensitive grammar (CSG) strings.
Interpolated Augmented LLMs (IALLMs) recognize CFG and IXG and also a significant portion (up to 44%) of CSG sentences.
The transition from single-stack to multi-stack memory in the automata hierarchy corresponds to the transition from language to logic abilities.
future_direction: Explore architectural changes to provide separate external memory stores to expand transformers to higher computational tiers.
Investigate the broader space of specific hybrid architectures, including interpolations of neurosymbolic methods.
papers.abstract: Human language and logic abilities are computationally quantified within the well-studied grammar-automata hierarchy. We identify three hierarchical tiers and two corresponding transitions and show their correspondence to specific abilities in transformer-based language models (LMs). These emergent abilities have often been described in terms of scaling; we show that it is the transition between tiers, rather than scaled size itself, that determines a system's capabilities. Specifically, humans effortlessly process language yet require critical training to perform arithmetic or logical reasoning tasks; and LMs possess language abilities absent from predecessor systems, yet still struggle with logical processing. We submit a novel benchmark of computational power, provide empirical evaluations of humans and fifteen LMs, and, most significantly, provide a theoretically grounded framework to promote careful thinking about these crucial topics. The resulting principled analyses provide explanatory accounts of the abilities and shortfalls of LMs, and suggest actionable insights into the expansion of their logic abilities.

papers.title: Tokens, the oft-overlooked appetizer: Large language models, the distributional hypothesis, and meaning
papers.research_question: What is the impact of tokenization on large language model cognition, meaning construction, and bias, and how does the tokenization algorithm's objective function affect the model's internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that tokenization is a crucial but overlooked component that shapes LLM cognition, acting as a backdoor for bias and obscuring the distributional patterns necessary for meaning acquisition, and that the tokenization algorithm's objective function impacts the model's internal representations despite being insulated from the main system intelligence.
papers.conclusion: Tokenization is a fundamental architectural choice that impacts model cognition and meaning construction, and current alignment practices may not remediate issues introduced by tokenization, motivating a re-examination of tokenization techniques and their role in LLM architecture.
papers.key_findings:
Tokenization can act as a backdoor for bias and unwanted content, which current alignment practices may not remediate.
The tokenization algorithm's objective function impacts the LLM's cognition, despite being arguably meaningfully insulated from the main system intelligence.
Tokens create suboptimal semantic building blocks and can obscure the model's access to the necessary distributional patterns from human language.
The distributional hypothesis (DH) is sufficient for reasonably human-like language performance (MVP language) in LLMs.
Analysis of token vector trajectories through model layers provides insight into the information space within vectors corresponding to a single token.
future_direction: Exploring connections between the distributional hypothesis and Hebbian learning.
Investigating the potential for moving beyond token-based architectural choices to more open-ended architectures.
papers.abstract: Tokenization is a necessary component within the current architecture of many language mod-els, including the transformer-based large language models (LLMs) of Generative AI, yet its impact on the model's cognition is often overlooked. We argue that LLMs demonstrate that the Distributional Hypothesis (DH) is sufficient for reasonably human-like language performance (particularly with respect to inferential lexical competence), and that the emergence of human-meaningful linguistic units among tokens and current structural constraints motivate changes to existing, linguistically-agnostic tokenization techniques, particularly with respect to their roles as (1) vehicles for conveying salient distributional patterns from human language to the model and as (2) semantic primitives. We explore tokenizations from a BPE tokenizer; extant model vocabularies obtained from Hugging Face and tiktoken; and the information in exemplar token vectors as they move through the layers of a RoBERTa (large) model. Besides creating suboptimal semantic building blocks and obscuring the model's access to the necessary distributional patterns, we describe how tokens and pretraining can act as a backdoor for bias and other unwanted content, which current alignment practices may not remediate. Additionally, we relay evidence that the tokenization algorithm's objective function impacts the LLM's cognition, despite being arguably meaningfully insulated from the main system intelligence. Finally, we discuss implications for architectural choices, meaning construction, the primacy of language for thought, and LLM cognition. [First uploaded to arXiv in December, 2024.]

papers.title: Interpreting the Latent Structure of Operator Precedence in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the LLaMA 3.2-3B model encode operator precedence in its internal representations, and how does it perform intermediate computations for arithmetic expressions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate arithmetic computations are linearly encoded in the residual stream of LLaMA 3.2-3B, particularly after MLP blocks, and that operator precedence is encoded in specific embedding dimensions, which can be altered via partial embedding swap.
papers.conclusion: The model internally performs intermediate computations and encodes operator precedence in its representations, with specific dimensions identifiable and modifiable through interpretability techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate calculations appear in the residual stream and are detectable via logit lens, with peak detection in layers 18-19.
Linear probes show that intermediate computations are linearly encoded in activations after layer 0.
Attention ablation in early layers significantly impairs accuracy and reduces intermediate computation detection.
Operator precedence is linearly encoded in embeddings after the attention layer, as shown by high probe accuracy.
Partial embedding swap can modify model predictions by swapping high-impact dimensions between operators.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities but continue to struggle with arithmetic tasks. Prior works largely focus on outputs or prompting strategies, leaving the open question of the internal structure through which models do arithmetic computation. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs encode operator precedence in their internal representations via the open-source instruction-tuned LLaMA 3.2-3B model. We constructed a dataset of arithmetic expressions with three operands and two operators, varying the order and placement of parentheses. Using this dataset, we trace whether intermediate results appear in the residual stream of the instruction-tuned LLaMA 3.2-3B model.
